points.t: Dry, cracked, scaly or blistering hands, often worse with work, cold weather or frequent washing.
Barrier breakdown from irritants, plus delayed allergy in some; atopy lowers the threshold.

Emollient after every wash, soap substitute, cotton-lined gloves, potent topical steroid in short bursts; patch-test referral if persistent; specialist alitretinoin or delgocitinib for severe disease.
Occupational disease (work advice, RIDDOR awareness), secondary infection or eczema herpeticum, and tinea manuum treated as eczema.

points: Repeated exposure (wet work, detergents, solvents, alkaline cement, friction, abrasion, occlusive gloves) strips stratum-corneum lipids and damages keratinocytes → **↑ transepidermal water loss**, barrier failure.
Damaged keratinocytes release IL-1α, TNF-α and other cytokines → innate inflammation; cumulative sub-threshold insults add up ("cumulative ICD").
Repetition drives **hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and lichenification**; in darker skin, **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** is prominent.
Risk modifiers: atopy/filaggrin loss-of-function, low humidity/winter, hot water, dominant-hand exposure.
**Rubber/leather gloves** — thiurams, carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole (rubber accelerators); chromate in leather.
**Epoxy resins, acrylates, isothiazolinone preservatives, solvents/degreasers, hand cleansers with abrasives.**
**ICD:** finger webs, dorsal hands, fingertips ("pulpitis"), ring site ("ring dermatitis"), dominant hand worse; glazed, fissured.
**Atopic hand eczema:** dorsal hands/wrists, history of flexural eczema/asthma/hay fever, onset in childhood/youth.
**Hyperkeratotic palmar eczema:** thick, fissured central palms, middle-aged men, little itch — closely mimics psoriasis.
both hands (dorsal/palmar/webs/nails), wrists, feet (tinea, pompholyx, psoriasis), scalp/elbows/nails (psoriasis), flexures (atopy).
for mycology if any scale is asymmetric or treatment-resistant (tinea manuum is a real possibility in a manual worker).
only if immediate (type I) symptoms — latex or food proteins (protein contact dermatitis/urticaria). Prick testing is for type I reactions; patch testing for type IV.
Diagnosis of ICD is largely **by exclusion** (negative/irrelevant patch tests + irritant history).

cards.name: Palmoplantar psoriasis
cards.clue: Sharp margins, thicker silvery scale, symmetrical, nails, psoriasis elsewhere, family history; can coexist (Koebner from work trauma)

cards.name: Tinea manuum
cards.clue: Usually **one hand**, white scale in creases, contiguous palm–dorsum spread, tinea pedis/nails; scrapings positive

cards.name: Keratolysis exfoliativa
cards.clue: No itch, no erythema, collarettes, summer

cards.name: Pompholyx
cards.clue: Recurrent crops of deep itchy vesicles

cards.name: Scabies
cards.clue: Burrows in finger webs/wrists, nocturnal itch, contacts

cards.name: Lichen planus / secondary syphilis / mycosis fungoides

items.t: Painful punched-out erosions or sudden worsening: **eczema herpeticum**, same-day.
Work-related dermatitis: advise occupational health, document exposures, patch-test referral.
One-sided scaly hand with tinea pedis (‘two feet, one hand’): scrape for **tinea manuum** before steroids.

pearls.t: Most chronic hand eczema relapses if exposure continues — success = protection + adequate steroid + maintenance, not steroid alone.
Fingertip-unit guide: one FTU covers both sides of one hand.
Thin palmar skin is uncommon — palms tolerate very potent TCS better than other sites, but dorsal hands thin easily; review every 4 weeks.
Dominant-hand predominance, ring-site eczema, and finger-web involvement → irritant. Dorsal hand + wrist cut-off at glove cuff → think glove allergy.
Always look at the **feet** in a hand rash.

Healthcare hand hygiene: prefer alcohol rub when hands not visibly soiled, dry hands fully before gloving, emollient at breaks and end of shift, report skin problems early (NHS staff hand-dermatitis pocket guides support this).
Concise answers to the six key questions, drawn from UK guidance.
One-liner: *acute = wet (erythema, oedema, vesicles, oozing); chronic = dry (scale, thickening, lichenification, fissures, pigment and nail change).*
